name: The state of context engineering 2026 (Redis)
date_published: Published August 2026 (report PDF filename carries date stamp 260803, i.e. 2026-08-03) [uncertain]
claim_value: 97% of surveyed IT/AI infrastructure leaders say context engineering is important to AI success, but only 4% have actually built the systems for it. Related figures: 73% agree agents fail more often from broken context than from broken models; 83% believe fresh context matters more than larger models; 81% operate at an 'ad hoc or exploratory' maturity stage; 80% of AI projects reportedly stall on data, governance, or infrastructure gaps.
claim_definition: A self-reported opinion survey of IT and AI infrastructure leaders on context-engineering maturity, belief vs. implementation gaps, and barriers to production AI agents, commissioned and published by Redis as a lead-generation/thought-leadership report.
reproducibility: Not applicable in the benchmark sense. No code or eval harness involved; this is a leader-opinion survey. Critically, the published report page and PDF do not disclose sample size, respondent count, job titles, company sizes, industries, or survey timeframe, so even the survey's own rigor cannot be independently checked.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: Yes. Redis sells caching and vector/agent-memory infrastructure directly implicated by the report's conclusions: Redis Iris ('real-time context for agents'), Redis LangCache (token-cost caching), Redis Agent Memory, Redis Context Retriever, and Redis Data Integration (CDC for 'fresh' data). The report's named barriers (latency, staleness, fragmented vector stores, lack of a unified memory layer) map near 1:1 onto Redis's product lineup, and the report explicitly recommends investing in 'context engine' infrastructure now.
conflict_notes: The 82% figure logged in article_ideas.md (09-27 entry: '82% of IT and data leaders agreeing prompts alone no longer suffice') does NOT appear anywhere in Redis's 'State of Context Engineering 2026' report. A direct fetch of the Redis report page found no instance of '82%'; the closest adjacent figures are 83% (fresh context beats bigger models) and 81% (early maturity stage / context called 'very important'). Web search results instead attribute the exact 82% wording to a separately-named '2026 State of Context Management Report', which is the DataHub-style report already flagged elsewhere in this research set, not Redis's. Secondary coverage (e.g. aggregator blog posts) sits the Redis 97%/4% stat and the 82% DataHub-style stat in the same paragraph without distinguishing publishers, which is likely how the two numbers got conflated in circulation. Conclusion: the 82% stat does not originate with Redis; it is being cross-attributed from a different vendor survey.
relationship: Supports the 'prompt engineering is dead, context engineering is what matters now' framing, and explicitly invokes external validation: the report cites Gartner's July 2025 line that 'context engineering is in, and prompt engineering is out.' Redis's own framing goes further than a simple prompt-to-context handoff, arguing models themselves are 'no longer the constraint' and that infrastructure (context graphs, event-driven sync, governance tooling) is the real bottleneck, a framing that happens to justify Redis's product category.
derivative_of: Builds rhetorically on Gartner's 2025 'context engineering is in' advisory and the broader 2026 context-engineering discourse (including Anthropic's MCP donation to the Linux Foundation, cited in the report as a sign of 'hardening standards'). It is not a replication or extension of DataHub's report; the two appear to be independent vendor surveys that reach structurally similar belief-vs-execution conclusions, which is itself notable (two self-interested vendors converging on a 'buy infrastructure now' message) but means the 82% should not be read as corroborated across both.
register: enterprise IT buyer (the report explicitly surveys 'IT and AI infrastructure leaders' and is pitched at production AI/agent decision-makers, not individual practitioners or academics)
notes: Redis's own report is internally rich with granular stats (dozens of percentages broken out by maturity stage) but discloses no methodology (no N, no respondent roles, no dates of fielding), which should discount confidence in all of its figures, including the ones that are real. Separately, the specific 82% figure widely cited alongside this report in secondary sources belongs to a different publisher's survey, not Redis's; any citation that attributes the 82% figure to Redis's 'State of Context Engineering 2026' report is incorrect.
new_angle: Corrects the attribution: the 82% stat in article_ideas.md's 09-27 entry traces to a report other than this one (most likely the DataHub-style 'State of Context Management' report already flagged for its own 82%/83% internal discrepancy), not to Redis. It also adds a second, independently-commissioned vendor survey with its own headline gap-stat (97% belief vs. 4% built) and its own undisclosed methodology, useful as a second data point for the essay's broader point that these survey stats are vendor-manufactured and should not be treated as corroborating evidence just because multiple vendors cite similar-sounding numbers.
